GitHub Octoverse 2026. I'm at GitHub Universe today (GitHub gave  me a free ticket through their "GitHub Stars" program). EVP Jay Parikh just announced this year's Octoverse report, and highlighted these numbers in particular:

This is a pretty stark representation of the impact of agentic engineering on GitHub. In 2026, merged pull requests tripled in less than a year to 220 million per month. Commits more than tripled to 7.38 billion per month, with most of that increase in the second half of this year. New repository rate doubled this year, to 30.3 million per month.

The report includes new numbers by industry, and breaks out numbers for repositories that involve "interoperability or reverse engineering". The methodology section includes notes about how they did this:

Top countries by pushes to public repositories, adjusted by profile location. Pushes from each country were summed across the Octoverse year. To adjust for biases caused by VPN usage, LLM classification was used to extract the ISO 3166-1 alpha-2 code from the profiles of GitHub users who contributed pushes during this period [...]
Industry. Public repositories created 2022 to 2026 were sorted into NAICS sectors by a fine-tuned multilingual embedding model using name, description, topics, and README, from random samples per year. [...]
Interoperability. Counts public repositories created each year whose name, description, topics, or README mention interoperability or reverse engineering, or related terms, such as clean room implementation, drop-in replacement, or protocol re-implementation.

blocks.text: 28th October 2026

I’ve written before about how November 2025 was an inflection point for coding agents—the point where Opus 4.5 and GPT-5.1 crossed a tipping point that meant their respective coding agents became reliable daily drivers for software engineers. I think we’ve reached a new inflection point in October 2026, and this time it’s for vibe coding computer games.
Tree Appreciator
Emberwick
Battle Drones
Pumpkin Farmer, aka Quarter Sun Cove
Four times as insulting
What happens if someone actually puts the work in?
You should build a game!
Claude Opus 5.5 in particular exhibits meaningful improvements in several areas needed to build a compelling game:
3D modeling
Music generation (see Scrimshaw Jukebox)
Game design (!)

That last one is particularly important. Models have been able to create something that looks like a game for quite a while now, as seen in my previous experiments. The challenge has been getting to a game that’s actually fun to play.

Game design is a deep subject area. I won’t pretend to be well versed in it—I know enough to have respect for it as a craft. Creating a novel, compelling gameplay loop which challenges players at the right level and provides a satisfying learning curve is a fine art. I didn’t think the models could do it.
Then I tried telling Claude Opus 5.5 to “Make it a LOT more fun”... and it did.
In the past few weeks I’ve vibe coded (in the classic sense of the term—no looking at the code at all) four games that I’ve genuinely enjoyed playing.

I attended Foo Camp in Berkeley over the weekend and met several people who were having similar experiences. Building games that play well is shockingly easy now. The new challenge is coming up with concepts for games that are novel and delightful and that wouldn’t exist without AI assistance.

I haven’t done an exhaustive study, but my current impression is that GPT-6 Astra isn’t quite there yet. It can absolutely build a game, but its sense of fun doesn’t match that of Opus 5.5. I expect OpenAI will get there by the end of the year.

Here are the four game projects that have convinced me that the models are now capable of producing fun games with very little guidance. All four are built in HTML and JavaScript and run entirely in the browser.
Tree Appreciator
The smallest game I found to be genuinely delightful is Tree Appreciator. I used the regular Claude chat interface for this—it didn’t even need Claude Code.
I built this on a whim while we were driving along Skyline Boulevard looking at trees. My prompt was:

Build a three js game called "Tree appreciator" - it shows you two algorithmically generated trees and the game mechanics is about appreciating the differences between them. Think hard about how to make sure it is both fun and beautiful.
I’ve found that telling models to use three.js works really well. Claude doesn’t have its own image generation model but is capable of building full-color 3D models that look and feel excellent.

This game required no iteration or follow-up prompting at all—I got the game in a single shot. It gave me back a charming little mobile-friendly spot-the-difference game. You can play that here. Here’s the chat transcript that built it.
It’s pleasingly relaxing. The graphics are fun, and collecting trees that you have completed in a “herbarium” provides a nice, cosy sense of accomplishment.
Emberwick
This was a more ambitious project that I again built using regular Claude chat. I started out by building an experimental prototype of an engine for a top-down fantasy RPG:

Build a demo game engine three.js which is a top down (but at an angle) RPG - the player gets to move through the world with one or two companions. Create a fantasy village setting that demonstrates walking around outside and then shows how when the player enters a building the wall between the player and the camera goes transparent so the user can see what is happening
Add some NPCs and plenty of furniture and different types of building some with an upstairs - be creative, make it look great
Here’s that first version. It worked really well!
I was inspired to increase my ambitions:

Make it not so flat - the buildings are great but the landscape itself is completely flat at the moment, fix that
Add basements to two of the buildings with a tunnel system joining them below the village
Add the start of a rocky mountain on one side of the village containing a cave with a sleeping troll
Here’s that version.
When that produced a good result, I decided to push it all the way:
Now turn this into an actual game - quadruple the size of the playable area, introduce fun game mechanics, add a plot that isn't too cliche, some twists, a magic system, make it really good
We’re back to prompts like “make it really good” here! Asking for a plot that “isn’t too cliche” seemed to work too—it’s a bit cliché, but still novel enough that I enjoyed following the story.

Unlike Tree Appreciator, this took quite a bit of additional playtesting and prompting to get to a finished version. This was mainly due to gameplay problems—things like a character not being in the right place to complete a quest because a different story element had caused them to move to another location.
Here’s that final game. It has a full story that takes about 15 minutes to play through.
There’s even an experimental level editor if you want to drop in your own houses, furniture, and landscape features.

Once it was all working (and I’d iterated through some gameplay bugs), I played it through from start to finish and found myself emotionally affected by the ending! I’m somewhat embarrassed by this, because everything in this game—the graphics, the plot, the characters, the music, the dialog—came from the model. My creative input was pretty much just “it’s a fantasy village and there’s a troll asleep in a cave”.
Here’s the full shared Claude chat in which I built this game.
I also fed that same initial sequence of prompts through ChatGPT GPT-6 Pro. Here’s the transcript and the finished game for comparison. It looks great, but I don’t think it plays nearly as well.
Battle Drones

This is by far my most successful project, which I wrote about last week. It’s a Command & Conquer-style Real-Time Strategy game where two robot armies (or four as of Saturday) build units, harvest scrap, and battle over territory.
This is also the project that convinced me that Opus 5.5 knows what “fun” is.
The first versions were built back in July using Claude Fable 5. It got me to a workable 2D Command & Conquer-style game, but it wasn’t great to play.
I prompted Opus 5.5 to “Make it a LOT more fun” and then later to “Port this game to three.js” and the game was transformed. There’s a blow-by-blow account (prompts included) in my write-up.

Today, Battle Drones has 2-4 player multiplayer (via a vibe coded WebSockets relay server), medals, replays, seven maps, a random map generator, and a set of “mutators” that add variants of the rules.

It also lets different LLMs play against each other, using a mode where the game advances five seconds and then pauses to give different models time to interpret the new game state and line up their next set of commands. Here’s a replay of Claude Haiku 5.5 vs. GPT-6 Luna:
Battle Drones is a particularly good example of Opus 5.5’s ability to create 3D models. This page lets you browse all of the models in the game.

I released Battle Drones under the Apache 2.0 License last Tuesday. On Wednesday Gabriel Turpin released Panache (screenshots here), a fork of Battle Drones that reimagined the game for steampunk 1900s Belle Époque France, with new models and music and an animated intro sequence. Open source at work!
Pumpkin Farmer, aka Quarter Sun Cove
I live in Half Moon Bay, California, home of the annual Half Moon Bay Art and Pumpkin Festival, which includes a giant pumpkin weigh-off competition.

I decided to try building a game that wasn’t just a cheap imitation of something that already existed, so I set out to create a game about farming pumpkins, growing giant pumpkins, and handling the rush of the October pumpkin season.
I called it “Quarter Sun Cove”.

I’m still iterating on this project, but it’s shaping up quite nicely. It’s a cosy farming simulator where you spend the year tending to your giant pumpkin and planting out regular-sized pumpkins for sale in October, then sell pumpkins during pumpkin season and enter your giant pumpkin in the weigh-off.

Every character in it is a (vegetarian) animal. The mayor of the town is a pelican. You can be a pelican, skunk, raccoon, possum, beaver, coyote, fox, owl, sea otter, or harbor seal. Those species all later show up (accompanied by their children) to buy pumpkins from you.
It’s absurdly cute.

You can play the latest version here. I’m not convinced by the game mechanics yet—it’s actually quite complicated: you have to decide when to plant pumpkins such that they will become ripe at the weekends in October with the most visitors.
Here’s the initial brainstorming session, which resulted in this spec file. Then I had Opus 5.5 Ultracode burn millions of tokens and nearly two days building it.

I told Claude to “surprise and delight the user frequently” and the result is so many little details and easter eggs. There are mischievous raccoons, an elephant seal that runs the weigh-off, harbor seals that roll their pumpkins back into the ocean, a wandering goat, and superstitions about growing giant pumpkins that sometimes come true.

This isn’t my best game yet—it’s not as fun to play as Battle Drones—but it represents the kind of game I want more of: weird, fun, uniquely personal—something that wouldn’t have been built in the before-times.
Four times as insulting
If you are offended by AI-generated art, AI-generated music, AI-generated writing, and AI-generated code, I have bad news for you: vibe coded games combine all of those at once.

The wider games community already has an aversion to AI-generated assets in games. This has been a growing issue over the past few years as tools like Midjourney have enabled developers to generate assets for their projects. This IGN story covering complaints about slop in Valve’s Steam Next Fest is a good recent example.
We now have games where everything—code, assets, dialog, and even the game design itself—can be outsourced to the models. And the results don’t suck!

Building a computer game used to be one of the most challenging projects in all of software development, combining a diverse range of skills and requiring intense focus and effort over many months or even years. And now here I am spitting out a playable multiplayer RTS by prompting on my phone!

I expect that, as we’ve already seen with programming, this will result in a split. Some players will refuse to have anything to do with games that were built in this way. Others may embrace this as opening up game development to a much wider audience. I lean in that direction!

I certainly won’t be entering any of my vibe coded games in traditional game jams or competitions—I don’t feel like I’ve earned that right. We’ll likely see new avenues emerge for vibe game developers to compare their projects.
What happens if someone actually puts the work in?

The thing I find both exciting and shameful about this is that I have got interesting results from so little creative input. The projects I’ve described here are loosely ordered by how much effort I’ve put into them. Not a single project represents more than four hours of my work (plus many more hours of Claude Code churning away by itself).

Now imagine what could be achieved by anyone who takes this seriously, invests significant creative time, applies better taste in game design, and then playtests and iterates on the result until it’s as good as they can make it.
I want to see games that wouldn’t have existed without these new tools.
You should build a game!
Building games in this way is so much fun. It’s the perfect application for vibe coding because it’s so low stakes: how much damage can you cause with a bug in a personal vibe coded game project?
(OK, you can do some damage... my attempt at audio-based multiplayer gave my wife Natalie a nasty headache!)

All of my games so far have been HTML and JavaScript using static hosting (generally GitHub Pages or Cloudflare Pages). Modern browsers—including mobile browsers—are incredibly capable. Frontier models already know libraries like three.js and Phaser. I’m finding these mobile web games to be indistinguishable from the native experience, at least for the kinds of games I’m trying to build.
I suggest starting with a prompt like this:
Build a mobile-friendly three.js game where...

This works on both chatgpt.com and claude.ai—you don’t even need to fire up a full coding agent. As one last example, here’s “Build a mobile-friendly three.js game where a mouse has to hide from a cat” by Claude Opus 5.5 Extra and by GPT-6 Extra High.
Switch to Codex or Claude Code once your project passes the proof-of-concept phase.
And if the game isn’t fun enough, add this:
Make it a LOT more fun

articles.title: Getting good at AI takes time and practice
articles.titleZh: Getting good at AI takes time and practice
articles.summary: Getting good at AI takes time and practice

blocks.text: Many people think1 that getting “good at AI” is trivial. Sure, with some early models there were tricks you had to learn,2 but current models don’t need them. Even if there are different tricks3 that work on current models, the next generation will render them obsolete, so why bother? Just tell the model what you want it to do.

This take is particularly popular with the anti-AI crowd, who scoff4 at the idea that AI-reluctant people are being left behind, or that it might be irresponsible to advise other engineers to avoid AI use entirely. According to them, if AI does ever become capable enough to be worth using, they’ll be able to start using it with no learning curve. Is that right?
No. Like most things, getting good at using AI isn’t just about clever tricks. It requires developing long-term skills5, which takes time and practice.
Supplying the right context

One failure mode I’ve seen with people who are new to AI is expecting it to read their mind: for instance, asking it to “solve my issue” without ever saying what the issue is, or asking it about some Slack-related problem without actually connecting your agent to Slack. Agents are flexible and will try their absolute hardest to guess what problem you’re facing and how to solve it, but the guesses will be largely wrong. Skilled AI users will pick up on the fact that the agent is missing key context and backtrack.

Skilled AI users will also reflexively include why they want to achieve their current goal, so that the agent has enough context to make decisions. This is often non-trivial: most of us know what we want to do but have to take a second to think about the broader reasons behind it.
Knowing what the model can and can’t do

AI capabilities are weird: they are very good at some tasks and very bad at others, and it’s hard to predict which task falls into which category. For instance, I know that I can ask an agent to come up with new architectural ideas for how to structure a service, but that I shouldn’t ask it to come up with new features that the service can offer. Worse still, there is a third category6 of tasks that AI models are bad at but can be prompted into being good: for instance, writing PR descriptions.

Of course, this changes with new models, but less than you’d think. In general, new models get much better at the tasks the old models were already good at, and a little better at the tasks the old models sucked at. So developing a sense of what AI can and can’t do is a surprisingly durable skill.

Really internalizing what the model can do is trickier than it sounds. For instance, I initially struggled to set up MCP servers for GitHub Copilot before realizing7 I could just ask Copilot to install its own MCP servers. I now reflexively ask AI agents to do local testing of changes — standing up servers, hammering them with curls, running through variations and edge cases — but it took me a while to realize I could ask for that. I have only just started scheduling a job for 6am my time for an agent to go through messages that have come in from different timezones and do some preliminary investigation. What other capabilities8 am I leaving on the table?
Knowing what mistakes the models make

Reviewing AI-generated code is a substantially different skillset from reviewing human-written code. There are whole categories of bugs — off-by-one errors, for instance — that human-written code is prone to but AI-generated code is not. Similarly, there are mistakes that are rare in human-written code but are very common in AI-generated code. I’ve written about how these tend to be mistakes of misalignment: over-engineering some areas that humans would know aren’t important, or trading off important requirements in order to satisfy made-up ones, and so on.

Reviewers used to human-written code are often dazzled by the superficial fluency of AI-generated code. It’s always exhaustively commented and tested and uses sophisticated language features. If a human programmer produced code like this, you’d be inclined to trust their judgment that a mutex is required in this case — but with an AI programmer, you ought to be very suspicious about new mutexes, which are often introduced to satisfy completely insignificant edge cases.
Rapidly skim-reading AI slop

This skill is kind of silly, but it’s so practically important I have to include it. AI models produce a lot of useful output, but it’s often lost in a thick forest of verbiage. Once you’ve read enough of it, you can sort of just let your eyes flow over the phrasing until you get to the specific claims and evidence. blocks.text: One of the many small pleasures of my job is when someone else writes a good take on a subject that I have been meaning to write myself. Occasionally this stings, because it was something I really wanted to write myself. But usually it’s just awesome, because it’s an article I wanted to exist, didn’t really want to do the work of writing myself, and now it exists and I can just link to it, perhaps with commentary. It’s like finding money on the ground or in the pocket of a jacket you haven’t worn in months.
That’s what happened yesterday with Glenn Fleishman’s “Why Notes Will Never Let Us Edit Markdown”, and my link to it. Found money!

But one of the reasons I’d been procrastinating on writing about Apple Notes and its growing support for Markdown import/export and copy/paste is that Notes is built around a text formatting idea that, to my knowledge, doesn’t really have a name. And without a name, it’s hard to write about. I’m going to suggest calling it prestructured WYSIWYG.

Apps like Apple’s Messages and especially Notes exemplify prestructured WYSIWYG, and I’m a huge fan of the idea. It’s low-key one of the best ideas and trends in software design of the last 15 years or so. Messages lets you apply WYSIWYG spans of character styles like bold and italics, but you can’t choose typefaces or define your own styles. Notes takes this further, adding inline hyperlinks and predefined block styles like title / heading / subheading, monostyled (e.g. for code), and ordered and unordered lists. But there is no Font menu or preference setting in Notes or Messages to change the default typeface. The “Aᴀ” formatting popover in Notes doesn’t have a control to change the typeface, only its preset styles, all of which are rendered in your notes using Apple’s San Francisco system font family.1 That would have seemed not just weird but downright wrong back in the early decades of the Mac (the era Fleishman calls the “Mac Is Not a Typewriter” era, referencing Robin Williams’s groundbreaking book). In those days, text was either plain text (a string of characters, no style at all, like a typewriter) or rich text, and if it was rich text, you expected to choose any font (and size) you wanted.

That era of anything-goes WYSIWYG presented unavoidable problems. On the technical side, the list of fonts installed on my computer isn’t the same as the list of fonts on your computer. Each operating system comes with its own set of included fonts. And the sort of people most interested in selecting their own typefaces are exactly the same people who are most likely to install third-party fonts. That’s a technical problem that can’t really be solved. There’s also an aesthetic problem. Most people, given the ability to choose their own fonts, make terrible typographic choices.

Prestructured WYSIWYG solves both problems. You get the expressiveness of abstract semantic styles like bold, italics, and monospace, and you get larger sizes for headings. But you avoid both the “missing font” technical problems and the “terrible font” design choices. If you use Apple Notes or Messages, you better like Apple’s San Francisco system font family, because that’s what you’re going to get. It’s great for accessibility, because all the type sizes are relative, not absolute. And these preset styles largely map well to Markdown, which itself has no concern with font choices or specific text sizes.

Even if you’re a decent designer (or believe yourself to be), it’s liberating not to have a say in the matter in certain contexts. Note-taking is exactly such a context. Email ought to be another, but alas, full-fledged WYSIWYG gained a foothold there long ago, and now it’s entrenched. Constraints are sometimes freeing.

There is a huge but here. Notes, on the Mac and only on the Mac, does allow you to pick arbitrary fonts. Format → Font → Show Fonts (⌘T) shows the standard AppKit Fonts palette, and you can use that to change the font in a note to anything you want. I think this is historical baggage from earlier versions of the Notes app for Mac. Or maybe there are some Mac Notes users inside Apple who really do use this. Font choices made in Notes on the Mac are rendered on iOS and iPadOS, if the selected font is available. It even works for third-party fonts (which are quite complicated to install on iOS). Here’s a screenshot of a note with custom fonts that I made on my Mac, and the same note as it appears on iOS, where only some of those fonts are installed. But you cannot change custom fonts in Notes on iOS.

I can’t say Apple discourages you from dicking around with fonts in Notes on the Mac. It’s right there in the standard AppKit Fonts panel. But most casual Mac users don’t know about the standard AppKit Fonts panel. When they pick fonts in apps like Mail, TextEdit, and Pages, they do it from toolbars in the window. So Apple doesn’t encourage you to dick around with fonts in Notes on the Mac either. If they wanted to encourage it, there’d be a toolbar with a Font menu on the Mac, and it would be possible to change fonts on iOS too.

So I say it’s best to pretend that Apple Notes doesn’t support custom font choices. Let it go — even if, like me, it drives you crazy that Notes and only Notes uses that childish-looking alternative single-story “a” glyph in San Francisco. ↩︎

But there is no Font menu or preference setting in Notes or Messages to change the default typeface. The “Aᴀ” formatting popover in Notes doesn’t have a control to change the typeface, only its preset styles, all of which are rendered in your notes using Apple’s San Francisco system font family.1 That would have seemed not just weird but downright wrong back in the early decades of the Mac (the era Fleishman calls the “Mac Is Not a Typewriter” era, referencing Robin Williams’s groundbreaking book). In those days, text was either plain text (a string of characters, no style at all, like a typewriter) or rich text, and if it was rich text, you expected to choose any font (and size) you wanted.

That era of anything-goes WYSIWYG presented unavoidable problems. On the technical side, the list of fonts installed on my computer isn’t the same as the list of fonts on your computer. Each operating system comes with its own set of included fonts. And the sort of people most interested in selecting their own typefaces are exactly the same people who are most likely to install third-party fonts. That’s a technical problem that can’t really be solved. There’s also an aesthetic problem. Most people, given the ability to choose their own fonts, make terrible typographic choices.

Prestructured WYSIWYG solves both problems. You get the expressiveness of abstract semantic styles like bold, italics, and monospace, and you get larger sizes for headings. But you avoid both the “missing font” technical problems and the “terrible font” design choices. If you use Apple Notes or Messages, you better like Apple’s San Francisco system font family, because that’s what you’re going to get. It’s great for accessibility, because all the type sizes are relative, not absolute. And these preset styles largely map well to Markdown, which itself has no concern with font choices or specific text sizes.

Even if you’re a decent designer (or believe yourself to be), it’s liberating not to have a say in the matter in certain contexts. Note-taking is exactly such a context. Email ought to be another, but alas, full-fledged WYSIWYG gained a foothold there long ago, and now it’s entrenched. Constraints are sometimes freeing.

There is a huge but here. Notes, on the Mac and only on the Mac, does allow you to pick arbitrary fonts. Format → Font → Show Fonts (⌘T) shows the standard AppKit Fonts palette, and you can use that to change the font in a note to anything you want. I think this is historical baggage from earlier versions of the Notes app for Mac. Or maybe there are some Mac Notes users inside Apple who really do use this. Font choices made in Notes on the Mac are rendered on iOS and iPadOS, if the selected font is available. It even works for third-party fonts (which are quite complicated to install on iOS). Here’s a screenshot of a note with custom fonts that I made on my Mac, and the same note as it appears on iOS, where only some of those fonts are installed. But you cannot change custom fonts in Notes on iOS.

I can’t say Apple discourages you from dicking around with fonts in Notes on the Mac. It’s right there in the standard AppKit Fonts panel. But most casual Mac users don’t know about the standard AppKit Fonts panel. When they pick fonts in apps like Mail, TextEdit, and Pages, they do it from toolbars in the window. So Apple doesn’t encourage you to dick around with fonts in Notes on the Mac either. If they wanted to encourage it, there’d be a toolbar with a Font menu on the Mac, and it would be possible to change fonts on iOS too.

So I say it’s best to pretend that Apple Notes doesn’t support custom font choices. Let it go — even if, like me, it drives you crazy that Notes and only Notes uses that childish-looking alternative single-story “a” glyph in San Francisco. ↩︎

https://pluralistic.net/2026/10/15/enshittipedia/

https://pluralistic.net/2024/06/07/drip-drip-drip/#drip-off

blocks.text: These are easily the most comfortable headphones I've worn. I've literally had them clipped around my ears all day without noticing them.

The good folks at SoundPEATS have sent me their latest cans to wrap around my lugs. I'm a big fan of these new-style "clip on" headphones. Rather than encasing your ears, or sticking way down into the wax-mines, these clip over your ear. It isn't a tight grip like a paperclip - more like the gentle caress of a tender but firm lover who wants only to delicately pinch your ears.
Look - it's hard writing about this stuff, OK?! Grab a pair and try them; you'll see what I mean. Here's a picture of an attractive model to give you an idea.
Specs

All the usual things you'd expect from headphones. AAC and SBC audio codecs are standard, it'll also do LDAC - which will get you higher quality but at the expense of battery life and the ability to connect to multiple devices at once.
The case recharges via USB-C, the battery seems fairly chunky and will quick-charges the headphones. 10 minutes in the case will give them 3 hours of playback.
Each clip has a button - you can change what they do in the supplied app.
IPX6 should be good for wearing in the rain, but you can't go swimming in them.
Useful Features
We all know what headphones can do - play audio, provide a microphone, and let you control the audio coming from your device. The CC3 Pro also have a few other smart features.
Like most decent battery-powered headphones, they will automatically switch off after a predetermined period without use.
There's a privacy mode which adds an EQ filter to reduce sound leakage. It works, but does make the sound slightly murkier.
There's a button on each one - you can use the app to set actions for tap, double-tap, triple-tap, and long press.
The case supports wireless charging, so you can chuck it on any charging puck for a quick top-up.
Comfort

Outstanding. After a few minutes you will genuinely forget that you're wearing them. Shake your head as hard as you like and they will not fall off. Here's a genuine photo of me doing some manly exercises while wearing them.
Sound Quality

Excellent - with a couple of caveats. These are open-ear devices. You can hear the world around you. That is by design and is extremely useful if you need to be aware of your surroundings. You can't block out the world or do active noise cancelling. I was not a fan of the default EQ. The bass wasn't bassy enough for me. It's easy enough to change in the app - but that does require a login.
Voice quality when speaking on the phone was also good. The people I spoke to could hear me clearly and with minimal background noise.
Android
Piece of cake. Open the case, press the button on the back, they're ready to pair.
Sound quality was great, my voice transmitted just fine, and I could easily play/pause and adjust the volume.
Linux
Again, dead easy. Ubuntu detected and paired with them instantly.
The App

I've complained to SoundPEATS before about their lousy app. The best thing I can say about it is that you don't have to use it. It's handy for downloading the occasional firmware update and fiddling with the setting. But that's about it.

It obnoxiously insists on needing an Internet connection to change some settings. Stuck on a train in the middle of nowhere and want to adjust your EQ? Tough. Similarly, some functionality is gated behind a login wall - such as the custom EQ and custom sound effects.
Thankfully, the rest of the app is fairly simple to use and will work offline. You can adjust what the buttons do, for example:
Weirdly, you can also download other people's EQ settings.
There's also a firmware update and a bunch of other things to flick on and off.
Downsides
Other than the app, there are a few niggles which are only slightly annoying.
Firstly, they don't pause when you take them out of your ear. That's a feature which was on the first set of SoundPeats I had and is sorely missed.
Secondly, the default sound profile wasn't very bass heavy. A bit of fiddling in the app and they sounded much better.

While they do charge in either slot within the case, they're incompatible with previous SoundPeats cases. The risk with smaller manufacturers like this is that you won't be able to find a cheap replacement case if you need it.
Price
Launch price is about £75 / €80. That's getting towards the upper end of what I think is acceptable for headphones like this.
Readers of this blog can use code PRCC3PRO for an extra 10% off at Amazon UK or other international Amazon stores. The code should work from today until 30th November 2026.

Ultimately, these are ridiculously comfortable headphones. They won't block out the noise of the environment around you - but that's their selling point. You use these while cycling, wandering through the city, or any other time you need to be aware of your surrounding. If you can put up with the slightly shonky app, these are well worth the price.
Many thanks to SoundPeats for the review pair.

blocks.text: This is a real paper that actually exists

Assessing the Psychometric Properties of the Dynomight™ MBTI: A Comparative Analysis with the Original Myers-Briggs Type Indicator.
Journal of Psychology and Behavior Studies, 4(1), 27-37.
Zrari, A., & Sakale, S. (2024).

A cohort of n=77 participants consented to engage in the study, meeting the inclusion criteria of being currently enrolled at the Tulua institution and expressing willingness to participate in both the initial assessment and the follow-up session. To assess the longitudinal consistency of the Dynomight™ MBTI, a second administration of the test was scheduled six weeks after the initial session.

  […]

  Empirical findings, as delineated in Table 1, manifested significant positive correlations across all dichotomies, indicative of a substantial concordance between the two assessments. The correlation coefficient for the Introversion-Extroversion axis was notably high (r = .938, p < .01), suggesting a pronounced alignment in the measurement of this dimension. Comparable strong correlations were observed for the Sensing-Intuition (r = .879, p < .01), Feeling-Thinking (r = .862, p < .01), and Judging-Perceiving (r = .847, p < .01) axes, underscoring the Dynomight™ MBTI’s proficiency in mirroring the evaluative scope of the original MBTI across the core personality dimensions.
“Dynomight™” is repeated in text 77 times.
Yeast vaccines

More is Different has a post on yeast-based vaccines, describing both why yeast-based vaccines are cool (if not self-evident) and how IRB rules can violate free speech and bodily autonomy make self-experimentation difficult:

Buck submitted an Institutional Review Board (IRB) proposal to gain permission to bring home the yeast and then use them to brew beer for his own consumption. To his surprise, an institutional bioethics committee withdrew the proposal from the submission portal before it could even be considered by the IRB. The committee argued that self-experimentation is strictly forbidden. Buck says he can find no written policies to that effect. The committee also argued that Buck could not eat the yeast strain unless it was first registered with the FDA as an Investigational New Drug.

  […]

  Rather than continuing to fight the bioethics committee, Buck went to his home kitchen instead.

I applaud this, but I’m a little confused about what legal theory Buck is using. The National Cancer Institute is in Maryland, and Maryland has a state law that says that all human subjects research must have IRB approval. All, with no exceptions. Perhaps Buck does not live in Maryland, or believes this law is unenforceable and/or unconstitutional.

(Many institutions have policies that say that all human subjects research conducted by employees must have IRB approval, even if those employees do it at home in their free time. But as far as I can tell, the National Cancer Institute only requires this for research done as part of official duties.)
Not a Meat Eater FAQ
Erich Grunewald makes the case. I admire this post for its willingness to acknowledge tensions and to make real concessions.

Are you sure you’re not just falling for anthropomorphic bias? How do you know your compassion for animals isn’t a misfiring of caregiving instincts we have for infants?

  I agree that anthropomorphism is a real phenomenon that can distort our intuitions on these questions. […] Sentience probably exists on a spectrum, as a result of its having evolved gradually over millions of years. Since humans appear to possess the highest degree of sentience, it makes sense that our closest evolutionary relatives would be more sentient than distant ones.
Cross-sectional illustrations of Kowloon Walled City
Kowloon Walled City “was an extremely densely populated and somewhat lawless enclave within the boundaries of Kowloon City of former British Hong Kong.” Here are some cross-sectional illustrations:

As a libertarian-curious person, I wish these kinds of experiments turned out less epic-cyberpunk and more boringly utopian. Also, the amount of frolicking in these illustrations strikes me as statistically anomolous.
Destroy luggage, save lives
YES:

One place I’d like to see this implemented is airplane evacuation. If the safety announcements included “In the event of an emergency evacuation, any carry-on luggage you bring will be confiscated and destroyed. You will also be fined.” we would have more JAL 516 (379 occupants, zero deaths) and less Aeroflot 1492 or Emirates 521.
Escapes
This thread lists some excellent escape attempts.
East Germany balloon escape:

They calculated the weight of the eight passengers and the craft itself to be around 750 kilograms (1,650 lb). Subsequent calculations determined a balloon capable of lifting this weight would need to hold 2,000 cubic metres (71,000 cu ft) of air heated to 100 °C (212 °F). The next calculation was the amount of material needed for the balloon, estimated to be 800 square metres (8,600 sq ft).
Great Papago Escape:

At least some of the escapees expected severe punishment for escaping; they were aware that 50 Allied prisoners of war had been executed after escape by their German captors in Stalag Luft III. However, the Camp Papago Park escapees were only limited to bread and water rations for as many days as they were absent from camp.
George Gamow:

Gamow later said that his first two attempts to defect with his wife were in 1932 and involved trying to kayak: first a planned 250-kilometer paddle over the Black Sea to Turkey, and another attempt from Murmansk to Norway. Poor weather foiled both attempts, but they had not been noticed by the authorities.
Stanislav Kurilov, candidate for most interesting man in the world:

After sunset on December 13, in stormy weather, Kurilov jumped overboard from the stern of the cruise ship, with a snorkeling mask and fins. Luckily, he was neither immediately noticed by the crew, or struck by the ship’s propeller. Because of the strong currents, it took him three nights and two days to reach the land.
Why are art films so good?

A common theory is that modern literature has shrunk into itself. There was a time when literature overlapped with entertainment and was a major cultural force. But nowadays, to be taken seriously as “literature”, a book is (allegedly) required to be so spare/ambiguous/fragmented that it can only appeal to a tiny slice of the population. Everything else is considered low-class “genre fiction”.

You can arguably see the same phenomena in other places. For example, in the golden era of jazz, jazz was pop music, whereas modern jazz is mostly for jazz nerds. Many would claim something similar is happening with modern architecture, in visual art, and various parts of academia.

But does this theory fit with film? To some degree, yes. I personally think American movies peaked in the 1970s, when there was a strong overlap between “art movies” and “popular movies”. Since then, there’s been a bit of a bifurcation: Anora earned 20× less than Deadpool & Wolverine. Often, Anora and D&W would be shown in completely differnt theaters. And James Patterson novels are not a bad approximation of “Deadpool and Wolverine, except it’s a book”.

Still, I have a question: Why are art movies so good? Sure, some of them suffer from a similar disease as modern literature. (Namely having almost no plot and consisting mostly of long still shots in which no one talks and nothing happens.) But all of the recent winners of the Palme d’Or that I’ve seen are both “true art” and also very entertaining.
(For calibration: Shoplifters, Parasite, Titane, Anatomy of a Fall, Anora.)
What’s the deal? Is there something different about films vs. books that led to this different outcome?
Ultra-processed food
Ultraprocessed foods and obesity: Interpreting the evidence

This is a criticism of RCTs that compare diets with ultra-processed food against those without for weight loss. They argue that the results could be explained by traditional nutritional properties like caloric density, soft/hard food texture, sodium, or saturated fat, rather by food reward/palatability or the effects of processing itself. Worth reading, though I’m not sure the degree to which the people who ran those RCTs would disagree. (What would it even mean for some effects to be caused by “processing itself”?)
Packing
Many of us are obsessed with optimal solutions for packing squares into a larger ambient square.

I agree that this reveals something about god’s mindset when creating the universe. But what about packing three-dimensional cubes into a larger ambient cube? I can find some math but not a single visualization or compendium of solutions.
Grug
The Grug Brained Developer (c.f.) is now a book.
USSR photos to look at with your eyes
Photos of the Soviet Union Taken by Thomas T. Hammond, 1950s–1970s
Recommended. Narrative-resisting.
Ask me stuff

The world is lacking in text-based content. Instead of cursing the darkness, I have determined to raise my content/effort ratio. If you would like to aid me in this goal, you can ask me stuff using this form to hypothetically be answered in a future post.
Forbidden topics:
American politics after the year 2000
Aspartame
Plagiarism

Luckily, he was neither immediately noticed by the crew, or struck by the ship’s propeller. Because of the strong currents, it took him three nights and two days to reach the land.
Why are art films so good?

A common theory is that modern literature has shrunk into itself. There was a time when literature overlapped with entertainment and was a major cultural force. But nowadays, to be taken seriously as “literature”, a book is (allegedly) required to be so spare/ambiguous/fragmented that it can only appeal to a tiny slice of the population. Everything else is considered low-class “genre fiction”.

You can arguably see the same phenomena in other places. For example, in the golden era of jazz, jazz was pop music, whereas modern jazz is mostly for jazz nerds. Many would claim something similar is happening with modern architecture, in visual art, and various parts of academia.

But does this theory fit with film? To some degree, yes. I personally think American movies peaked in the 1970s, when there was a strong overlap between “art movies” and “popular movies”. Since then, there’s been a bit of a bifurcation: Anora earned 20× less than Deadpool & Wolverine. Often, Anora and D&W would be shown in completely differnt theaters. And James Patterson novels are not a bad approximation of “Deadpool and Wolverine, except it’s a book”.

Still, I have a question: Why are art movies so good? Sure, some of them suffer from a similar disease as modern literature. (Namely having almost no plot and consisting mostly of long still shots in which no one talks and nothing happens.) But all of the recent winners of the Palme d’Or that I’ve seen are both “true art” and also very entertaining.
(For calibration: Shoplifters, Parasite, Titane, Anatomy of a Fall, Anora.)
What’s the deal? Is there something different about films vs. books that led to this different outcome?
Ultra-processed food
Ultraprocessed foods and obesity: Interpreting the evidence

This is a criticism of RCTs that compare diets with ultra-processed food against those without for weight loss. They argue that the results could be explained by traditional nutritional properties like caloric density, soft/hard food texture, sodium, or saturated fat, rather by food reward/palatability or the effects of processing itself. Worth reading, though I’m not sure the degree to which the people who ran those RCTs would disagree. (What would it even mean for some effects to be caused by “processing itself”?)
Packing
Many of us are obsessed with optimal solutions for packing squares into a larger ambient square.

I agree that this reveals something about god’s mindset when creating the universe. But what about packing three-dimensional cubes into a larger ambient cube? I can find some math but not a single visualization or compendium of solutions.
Grug
The Grug Brained Developer (c.f.) is now a book.
USSR photos to look at with your eyes
Photos of the Soviet Union Taken by Thomas T. Hammond, 1950s–1970s
Recommended. Narrative-resisting.
Ask me stuff

American politics after the year 2000
Aspartame
Plagiarism

blocks.text: In C++/WinRT, there are two ways of creating objects that you yourself implement.

For the purpose of this discussion, let Impl be the class you wrote that implements a Windows Runtime object. If you are implementing something that was declared in an IDL file, it will be the winrt::Namespace::implementation::ClassName for the instance object or it will be the winrt::Namespace::factory_implementation::ClassName for the factory object. If it wasn’t declared in an IDL file, then it is the class that you manually derived from winrt::implements.

One way to create the object is to use make<Impl>, which creates the implementation object and then returns the Windows Runtime projection version of that object. (If Impl is manually-derived from winrt::implements, the projection is the first implemented interface.)

From that Windows Runtime projection, you can regain access to the implementation object by doing get_self<Impl>(projected), if you want to access things in the implementation object that aren’t exposed in the projection.

Alternatively, you use make_self<Impl>, which creates the object but returns a winrt::com_ptr<Impl> instead of a projection. You can then access things in the implementation object from that winrt::com_ptr, and convert it to the projected type with the * operator.
Which one you choose depends on where you want to go first.

If you are first going to access  non-projected public members of the implementation class, use the -> operator on the com_ptr<Impl>. For example, you might want to set up the object before returning the projection.
But if you are just going to use the projection, you can take the direct route instead of going the long way.
In this case, you don’t need to pass through the implementation type.
My guess is that the people who go the long way don’t realize that there are two ways. They learned only one way and just rely on it even if there’s a shorter way.

blocks.text: The classification of finite simple groups (CFSG) has been called the biggest theorem in mathematics. It is big, not necessarily in terms of its importance, but in the sense that its proof developed over the course of decades and thousands of pages of journal articles.

Two days ago Axiom announced it had formalized the proof of CFSG in 43.1 million lines of Lean. If you click on the link for the accompanying paper, you’ll find that the title of the paper is The Unbalanced Group Theorem, not The Classification of Finite Simple Groups. Why is that?

The unbalanced group theorem (UGT) is a key component of the CFSG. In the course of their effort to formalize CFSG Axiom found counterexamples to an assertion that the 1986 proof of UGT depends on. The UGT, and the CFSG that depends on it, is correct, but the proof was flawed. Axiom formalized the entire CFSG but focused their paper on their new proof of the UGT.
What exactly does the UGT say? For that matter, what is a finite simple group?
A short post like this can only go into so much detail, but I’ll see what I can do.

A group represents some kind of symmetry. Groups can be built out of simple groups sorta like the way integers can be built out of primes. See more on the comparison between simple groups and prime numbers here.
The CFSG says that every finite simple group is cyclic, alternating, of Lie type, or sporadic. The UGT is a technical result used in proving that nothing is missing from this list of possibilities.
What does it mean for a group to be “unbalanced”? This depends on a few preliminary definitions.
Define O(G) to be the largest normal subgroup of G with an odd number of elements.
An element t in G is called an involution if it has order 2: t is not the identity but t² is.
The centralizer of an element t of a group G, written CG(t), is the set of elements of G that commute with t.
A group G is unbalanced if O(CG(t)) is a not a subgroup of O(G) for some involution t.
The UGT is a classification theorem for unbalanced groups.

blocks.text: Alongside package management, I follow new features and security fixes in source control clients and in the forges that host repositories, since a lot of what I build, like git-pkgs, reads git repositories and calls forge APIs. This Week in Package Management has been published every Saturday since May, and I kept putting git releases and forge news in its Elsewhere section.

Starting this week, I’m publishing that material as a separate roundup on Wednesdays. It covers clients like git, jj, gitoxide, Sapling, Mercurial and Git LFS, and forges like GitHub, GitLab, Forgejo, Gitea, Codeberg, sourcehut, Radicle and Tangled. Package managers resolving git dependencies and CI systems like GitHub Actions are covered in the Saturday post.

This first issue covers the fortnight since 11 October, with links from release feeds for those tools and forges, the Lobsters vcs tag, Hacker News and my boosts on Mastodon. In that fortnight Anthropic, GitHub, Entire and Enroute each published a post about rebuilding source control or git hosting for the volume of pushes and checkouts from coding agents.
Scaling

Redesigning source control at Anthropic (Anthropic Engineering) describes Scion, an in-house version control system that replaced git for the company’s monorepo in five months. Merges went from around 2,500 a day in May to over 30,000 a day in September. The main branch history is almost 100 GB, and CI performs around 25 million checkouts a day. Scion is designed for clients that are always online. The server stores changesets in a write-ahead log on Spanner and runs blame, history and merge queries server-side, and clients fetch only the trees and blobs they request through regional caches. Anthropic reports the new infrastructure uses 200x less CPU and memory than the git mirror fleet it replaced. In notes on the post, Simon Willison compares it to centralised systems like Subversion.

Anthropic’s Scion is heavily inspired by Mononoke (sunshowers) points out that Scion’s “derived data” for fast blame and history queries matches the design of Mononoke, the server side of Meta’s Sapling. The original post credited Sapling only for “hard-won lessons”. A follow-up compares Scion’s changesets with Mononoke’s Bonsai changesets. Anthropic has since updated its post with more detail on the projects Scion is based on.

The bridge to agent-scale Git infrastructure (Eleanor White and Victoria Dye, GitHub Blog) covers the move of GitHub’s repositories to Azure. Most repositories have two of their five replicas there, and Azure serves about half of Git traffic. Moving the busiest repositories was blocked by a repository-wide lock that every write held across a 25ms cross-region round trip. Spokes is switching to per-reference serialisation, so only writes to the same ref wait for each other, which gave 3-4x write throughput in internal tests. Object storage then joins the write quorum as a “virtual replica”, so read replicas can be stateless.

Entire, a new git forge from a company co-founded by former GitHub CEO Thomas Dohmke, is built for repositories where coding agents and people push to the same branches. Its git server replicates each repository across regions, and the company’s forgemark benchmark reports pushes up to 89x faster than GitHub and 6x faster than Cursor Origin. Review happens through Trails, which run configured checks and agent-run evaluations in Daytona or E2B sandboxes on every push instead of a pull request diff. Agent sessions and prompts are synced into the repository and indexed for later agents to search.

Everyone is doing Git on S3 wrong (Enroute) looks at the write-ahead log designs for git on object storage that followed Cursor’s Continuity. Those designs send every push to a repository through one primary, and every replica keeps a full copy of the repository on disk. Enroute keeps each repository’s refs and a list of immutable object layers in a Raft-replicated log. Packfiles are rewritten on ingestion so a read from object storage needs only a few requests, and Enroute reports more than 7,600 pushes per second into a single repository. Against stock git serving a repacked linux.git, full clones are about 17% slower and shallow clones more than twice as fast.
Releases

GitLab 19.5 makes the GitLab MCP server and GitLab Secrets Manager, built on OpenBao, generally available. Smaller changes include a commit count variable for commit message templates, and commits signed by revoked GPG identities now show as unverified.

Forgejo 17.0 resolves absolute links in rendered documents against the repository root, as other forges do, and deprecates action run webhook events in favour of workflow run events. It also adds a Donate button driven by FUNDING.yml, migration from Bitbucket Data Center, and opt-in invitations for organisation membership. Forgejo 17.0.1, 16.0.7 and 15.0.11 followed on 26 October as security releases. The main fix stops a pull_request_review event running an Actions workflow as trusted from an arbitrary commit, including one from a fork, by ignoring the unvalidated commit_id on the submitted review. 17.0.1 also carries bug fixes for 17.0.0, which the project had advised holding off from after reports of blocked pushes and merges.

GitRoot 0.5.0, a self-hosted forge with no database that is extended through WASM plugins, now references plugins by PURL with a checksum qualifier in place of separate URL, checksum and version fields. New per-forge and per-repository settings cap how many branches anonymous users can push before further anonymous pushes are rejected.

Pushin.eu, an invite-only forge hosted in the EU, shipped several releases this fortnight according to its changelog. 0.3.26 adds tag-based releases with a GitHub-compatible API and GoReleaser publishing, and 0.3.29 serves public repository files from raw.pushin.eu. 0.3.32 adds runner groups for self-hosted runners and removes the per-repository allow_persistent_runners setting.

forges (Daniel Roe) is a TypeScript version of my Go library git-pkgs/forge, with one interface for issues, pull requests, notifications, checks and webhooks across GitHub, GitLab, Bitbucket, Forgejo, Gitea, Gitee, Azure DevOps, Cursor Origin, Tangled, Pushin.eu and Sourcehut. Each provider declares which operations it supports, and the release notes show the capability changes per forge. 0.1.0 came out on 11 October, and 0.3.0 adds branch rules and review threads.

gt 0.1.0 replaces tea, Gitea’s command line tool, with a rewrite under a new name and repository. Every list and view command supports --json and --jq, and gt pr checkout and gt pr diff handle fork and AGit pull requests. It requires Gitea 28 or newer.
gitoxide 0.61.0 moves the plumbing crates to a standard std::error::Error compatible error type and improves tracing across commands, along with security fixes.
Security
Git LFS 3.8.1 fixes four CVEs:
unquoted arguments in remote commands sent over SSH
Cookie headers forwarded to other hosts after a redirect
an arbitrary program run from a malicious repository through line feeds in a submodule URL
an arbitrary program run from a malicious repository through a custom transfer adapter set in .lfsconfig

GitLab shipped two critical patch releases for integer overflows in its regular expression compiler that allowed unauthenticated code execution. The first, on 12 October, fixed CVE-2026-97229 in CI configuration patterns, and a 21 October release fixed CVE-2026-110264, which affects every version from 7.0 and was backported as far as 18.11.13. The underlying bugs are in Ruby’s Onigmo, whose fixes were in last week’s package management roundup.

Gitea 28.2.0 discloses 13 CVEs, two of them fixed in earlier releases. One fix limits which stored public keys an SSH certificate principal is matched against. Before the fix, matching against every stored key let a certificate authenticate as a different user.

git-annex 10.20261026 fixes CVE-2026-112818, a cross-repository exfiltration attack found by Joey Hess. A repository the victim clones can autoenable a special remote that points at the victim’s own private git-annex storage, so a later git-annex sync --content reads the private files and sends them to the attacker. After the fix, enableremote requires the special remote’s configuration to be verified, and git-annex refuses to send content to an unverified autoenabled remote.

Gheist (Rami McCarthy and Hila Ramati, Wiz) is a campaign that used stolen GitHub tokens to push a workflow to every reachable repository. The workflow writes repository secrets to its log in base32 so GitHub’s masking leaves them unredacted, and the attacker’s tool fetches the log over the API and deletes the run seconds later. GitHub’s hold on potentially malicious workflows in public repositories, in place since 28 July, blocked the payload there. Private repositories and GitHub Enterprise Server fall outside that hold, and Wiz observed successful runs and follow-on AWS activity from those.

An attacker took over a developer’s GitHub account and replaced OVHcloud CLI releases 0.11.0 to 0.15.0 with builds that read secrets from disk. Release immutability was turned off on the repository, so the attacker could overwrite the existing releases directly and skip CI.
GitHub

Push attribution, in limited preview for Enterprise customers, records the authenticated user who pushed each commit alongside the author and committer fields. A new “Committer must match pusher” ruleset condition accepts a push only when the committer matches one of the pusher’s verified email addresses.
During periods of unusual traffic, unauthenticated HTTPS clones and fetches of public repositories may require authentication, while SSH, authenticated HTTPS and pushes work as before.

GitHub CLI 2.103.0 adds gh auth login --expiring for refreshable tokens that expire within hours. Used as a git credential helper, it requires git 2.46 or newer, which discards a cached credential when it expires.

Repositories can now convert all their branch protection rules to rulesets in one step, with a preview before anything changes. A new repository_creation:write permission lets apps and fine-grained tokens create repositories with only that permission instead of full repository administration.
On the Files changed tab of a pull request, the whitespace visibility setting can be saved so it applies across pull requests, and new and deleted files now span both columns in split view.
Email notifications for push events have been retired because recipients could be added without consenting.
Elsewhere
Haxy, now in preview, is a local-first forge written in Zig that stores issues, pull requests and discussions as events on a haxy/events branch and serves a TUI over SSH alongside its web interface.

Making git hooks visible in fish shell (Chris R) ports Ned Batchelder’s zsh function, which lists a repository’s executable hooks when you cd into it, after Frank Wiles nearly fell for an attack hidden in a shared hooks folder.

jwz has created a GitHub repository whose only content is a README stating that XScreenSaver releases are published only as tarballs on the XScreenSaver website and that other repositories are unofficial.
Send links for next week to @[email protected].

A new “Committer must match pusher” ruleset condition accepts a push only when the committer matches one of the pusher’s verified email addresses.
During periods of unusual traffic, unauthenticated HTTPS clones and fetches of public repositories may require authentication, while SSH, authenticated HTTPS and pushes work as before.

GitHub CLI 2.103.0 adds gh auth login --expiring for refreshable tokens that expire within hours. Used as a git credential helper, it requires git 2.46 or newer, which discards a cached credential when it expires.

Repositories can now convert all their branch protection rules to rulesets in one step, with a preview before anything changes. A new repository_creation:write permission lets apps and fine-grained tokens create repositories with only that permission instead of full repository administration.
On the Files changed tab of a pull request, the whitespace visibility setting can be saved so it applies across pull requests, and new and deleted files now span both columns in split view.
Email notifications for push events have been retired because recipients could be added without consenting.
Elsewhere
Haxy, now in preview, is a local-first forge written in Zig that stores issues, pull requests and discussions as events on a haxy/events branch and serves a TUI over SSH alongside its web interface.

Making git hooks visible in fish shell (Chris R) ports Ned Batchelder’s zsh function, which lists a repository’s executable hooks when you cd into it, after Frank Wiles nearly fell for an attack hidden in a shared hooks folder.

jwz has created a GitHub repository whose only content is a README stating that XScreenSaver releases are published only as tarballs on the XScreenSaver website and that other repositories are unofficial.
